tagline: Not the ruined 13th-century Inverlochy nearby, but a Victorian baronial mansion Queen Victoria called the most beautiful and romantic place she had ever seen — now a 5-star Relais & Châteaux hotel below Ben Nevis
highlights: A different castle entirely from the ruined 13th-century Inverlochy Castle two miles away — this is a Victorian mansion built in 1863, with no historical connection to the medieval fortress beyond sharing its name and general area
Queen Victoria stayed a week in 1873 en route to Balmoral, sketching and painting the surrounding scenery, and later wrote that she had never seen a more beautiful or romantic spot

description:
Inverlochy Castle is one of two very different things sharing a name and a stretch of Highland scenery near Fort William, and it is worth being precise about which one this is. Two miles away stand the ruins of the genuinely medieval Inverlochy Castle — a 13th-century fortress managed by Historic Scotland, currently closed to visitors for conservation work. This Inverlochy Castle is a completely separate building: a Victorian country mansion constructed in 1863, with no architectural or historical continuity with the medieval ruin beyond proximity and a shared place name. Anyone researching a visit to the historic fortress should look elsewhere; this page covers the hotel.

The mansion was built for William Frederick Scarlett, 3rd Baron Abinger, on a private estate of 42,000 acres beneath Ben Nevis, Britain's highest mountain. The London architect George Hesketh designed the original Scots Baronial house, and in 1889 the Edinburgh firm of MacVicar Anderson enlarged it substantially, adding a four-storey tower with a turret and — notably for a remote Highland estate of the period — electric light and hot running water throughout. The result was a house built explicitly for aristocratic entertaining on a grand scale, set against one of the most dramatic mountain backdrops in Britain.

The house's most celebrated historical moment came in 1873, when Queen Victoria stayed for a week en route to Balmoral. She spent the visit sketching and painting the surrounding landscape and later recorded in her journal that she had never seen a more beautiful or more romantic place — a line the hotel still quotes today, and one that has shaped its identity as a destination as much for its setting as for the building itself. The Ben Nevis massif, visible from the grounds, provides the backdrop Victoria found so striking, and the same view remains the estate's defining feature.

The estate passed out of the Abinger family and eventually, in 1944, was sold to the Canadian industrialist Joseph Hobbs, who also owned the Ben Nevis Distillery nearby. It was Hobbs's son who converted the mansion into a hotel, and Inverlochy Castle received its first paying guests in 1969. The conversion preserved the house's grand public rooms and individually decorated bedrooms rather than subdividing them for volume, a decision that shaped the hotel's identity as an intimate, high-end property rather than a large-scale operation — it has never grown beyond 17 rooms.

Today Inverlochy Castle holds 5-star ratings from both the AA and VisitScotland and is a member of Relais & Châteaux, the global association of independently owned luxury properties recognised for exceptional food, service, and character. The house sits within its own grounds with walking paths and a walled garden, and the estate's remoteness — three miles from Fort William, with Ben Nevis dominating the skyline — is as much the draw as the building's Victorian grandeur. Non-residents are welcome to book a lounge meal, dinner, or the hotel's afternoon tea (served in one of the lounges, with a traditional and a Champagne option), making it possible to experience the house and its setting without booking an overnight stay, though reservations for dining are strongly advised given the property's small size.
history: William Frederick Scarlett, 3rd Baron Abinger, commissioned the original house in 1863 as a private residence on his 42,000-acre Highland estate near Fort William, engaging the London architect George Hesketh to design a Scots Baronial mansion befitting an aristocratic Highland retreat. Queen Victoria's week-long stay in 1873, en route to Balmoral, brought the house wider recognition; her journal entry praising the setting as the most beautiful and romantic she had encountered has remained attached to the property's identity ever since. In 1889, the Edinburgh architectural firm of MacVicar Anderson substantially enlarged the house, adding a four-storey tower with turret and modern conveniences including electric light and hot running water — improvements that placed the house at the forefront of Highland country house comfort for its era. The Abinger family's ownership ended in the mid-20th century, and in 1944 the estate was purchased by Joseph Hobbs, a Canadian industrialist who also owned the nearby Ben Nevis Distillery. Hobbs's son subsequently converted the mansion into a hotel, and Inverlochy Castle welcomed its first guests in 1969, beginning its current identity as one of Scotland's most decorated small luxury hotels.

faqs.question: Is this the same Inverlochy Castle managed by Historic Scotland?
faqs.answer: No. There are two separate Inverlochy Castles near Fort William. The genuinely medieval one — a 13th-century ruined fortress — is managed by Historic Scotland and sits about two miles from this hotel; it is currently closed to visitors for conservation work. This page covers the Victorian mansion built in 1863, now operating as a 5-star Relais & Châteaux hotel. The two buildings share a name and a general location but have no historical or architectural connection.

faqs.question: Can I visit Inverlochy Castle Hotel without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Non-residents are welcome to book a lounge meal, dinner, or the hotel's afternoon tea, served in one of the house's lounges. Reservations are strongly advised given the hotel's small size — it has only 17 bedrooms and the dining spaces are correspondingly intimate. There is no general walk-up access to the grounds or public rooms outside of a dining reservation.

faqs.question: What did Queen Victoria say about Inverlochy Castle?
faqs.answer: Following her week-long stay in 1873 while travelling to Balmoral, Queen Victoria wrote in her journal that she had never seen a more beautiful or more romantic place, having spent much of her visit sketching and painting the surrounding Highland scenery beneath Ben Nevis. The quote has remained closely associated with the property and its setting ever since.
